questions.q: What is the purpose of the `name` attribute in an `<input>` element inside a form, and what happens if you omit it?
questions.a: The `name` attribute assigns a unique identifier to the input field so that when the form is submitted, the server can associate the submitted value with that field (e.g., `name="email"` sends `email=user@example.com`). If omitted, the input's value is not sent with the form data at all — the server receives nothing for that field. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's just a label for the user") reveals confusion between the visible label (`<label>`) and the programmatic name used in data submission.

questions.q: Explain the difference between `method="GET"` and `method="POST"` in a form. Give one situation where you would choose POST over GET.
questions.a: GET appends form data to the URL as query parameters (visible, bookmarkable, length-limited), while POST sends data in the HTTP request body (not visible in URL, no practical length limit, more secure for sensitive data). Choose POST for login forms, payment details, or any submission that changes server state (e.g., inserting a database record). A wrong answer (e.g., "POST is always better") shows lack of understanding of idempotency and caching — GET is appropriate for search forms where bookmarking/sharing the query is desired.

questions.q: Compare radio buttons and checkboxes. When would you use each? If you have three radio buttons with the same `name` but different `value`s, what data is sent when the second one is selected?
questions.a: Radio buttons (`type="radio"`) allow exactly one choice from a group (same `name`); checkboxes (`type="checkbox"`) allow zero or more independent choices. Use radio for mutually exclusive options (gender, payment method); checkboxes for multiple selections (hobbies, toppings). If three radios share `name="color"` with values `red`, `green`, `blue`, and the second (green) is selected, the form submits `color=green`. A wrong answer (e.g., "all three values are sent") shows confusion about radio group behavior — only the selected radio's value is submitted.

questions.q: A student writes a form with two submit buttons: `<input type="submit" name="action" value="Save">` and `<input type="submit" name="action" value="Delete">`. The form's action is `/process`. When the user clicks "Delete", what data is sent to the server? Is this a good design? Justify.
questions.a: Clicking "Delete" sends `action=Delete` (only the clicked submit button's name/value pair is included). The server can check `$_POST['action']` (or equivalent) to decide whether to save or delete. This is a valid and common pattern for multi-action forms. However, it has a usability risk: if the user presses Enter in a text field, the browser may submit the first submit button ("Save") unintentionally. A better design might use separate forms or JavaScript to confirm destructive actions. A wrong answer (e.g., "both buttons' values are sent") shows ignorance of the rule that only the activated submit button contributes to form data.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: HTML forms are ______ sections of a web page that collect user input through various input elements (text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns, etc.) and send the data to a server for processing.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are building a "Student ______" page for your school's annual fest.
What is HTML forms? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: HTML forms are interactive sections of a web page that collect user input through various input elements (text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns, etc.) and send the data to a server for processing.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about HTML forms?
questions.a: Students often think the value attribute of a text input is the same as the placeholder.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) write complete HTML form code using appropriate input types and attributes for a given data collection scenario, and (2) explain the purpose of each attribute (name, value, required, placeholder, etc.) and how form data is submitted via GET/POST methods.
